title: Giving Measurements a Place
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Three thermometers give us three readings. Before we can calculate with them, we need to decide how those readings are stored, which position belongs to which thermometer, and what an operation should do to the collection.

title: Which Direction Are We Adding?
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: A table can hold several greenhouses across several days. Adding across a row answers a different question from adding down a column. We need to keep that distinction when we ask an array to calculate.

title: Preparing the Arrays We Need
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Botie needs a place for tomorrow's readings and a set of times at which to collect them. We can describe those arrangements directly instead of typing every repeated value ourselves.

title: Choose the Readings Without Losing Their Place
blurb: Botie may need one morning, a run of mornings, or selected greenhouses. We need to express each request precisely and know whether editing the selection will change the original report.

title: Put the Same Readings Into the Right Arrangement
blurb: A sensor may send one long sequence while a calculation expects rows. We need to change the arrangement without changing which measurements belong to each day and greenhouse.

title: One Reference for Many Rows
blurb: Each greenhouse has its own target temperature. We want to compare every day's readings with those three targets without copying the targets into a new table by hand.

title: Ask Each Row a Question
blurb: Botie needs the greenhouse readings that reached a temperature limit. A yes-or-no decision for each reading lets us select the relevant observations without losing their order.

title: Summarise a Report Without Losing the Question
blurb: Botie needs totals, typical readings, and the greenhouse that needs attention first. A value, a position, and an ordered report answer different questions, even when they come from the same array.

title: One Calculation for a Whole Report
blurb: Botie applies the same rule to many readings. We will first write the repeated steps, then express them with array operations while keeping the intermediate values and memory costs understandable.

title: Turn Several Measurements Into Several Predictions
blurb: A prediction can combine temperature and humidity with separate coefficients. Matrix operations let us apply that same rule to every greenhouse, then check how a fitted rule relates to its observations.

title: When Two Calculations Almost Agree
blurb: A tiny rounding difference, a missing observation, and a wrongly shaped result are different problems. We need checks that distinguish them before trusting a numerical answer.

title: Can We Repeat the Same Experiment?
blurb: Changing both a model and its sampled observations makes it difficult to explain a changed result. We need to keep track of the random choices so we can repeat a comparison.

title: Give a Reusable Calculation a Clear Contract
blurb: Copying a calculation into every exercise makes mistakes hard to repair. We will put the rule in a function, state what its inputs mean, and check it on more than one report.

title: Keep Enough of a Calculation to Run It Again
blurb: A printed table is not a complete experiment record. We will save arrays with their shapes and types, keep related arrays together, and check what survives when a report moves through a text file.

title: What Does One Row Represent?
blurb: Two identical-looking rows might be a duplicated import or two genuine observations. We need to establish a record's identity before cleaning a dataset or trusting its counts.

title: When a Measurement Is Missing
blurb: An empty thermometer reading does not mean the greenhouse was at zero degrees. We need to distinguish what was measured from what we supplied to keep a calculation working.

title: Categories Without an Invented Ranking
blurb: A roof can be glass, plastic, or mesh. Assigning those names arbitrary numbers can accidentally suggest a ranking. We need a representation that preserves category membership without inventing a numerical relationship.

title: When the End Is Beside the Beginning
blurb: The hour after 23 is zero, yet ordinary subtraction puts those hour numbers far apart. A repeating feature needs a representation that keeps its beginning beside its end.

title: What Could We Know at Prediction Time?
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: A model can appear remarkably accurate when a feature contains information that arrives after the decision. We need to reconstruct what was actually available when each prediction would have been made.

title: When the Important Class Is Rare
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: If almost every sensor is healthy, predicting healthy every time can look accurate while missing every failure. We need to inspect what the score says about each class.

title: What Must a Model Improve On?
blurb: A complicated predictor needs a simple comparison. Before fitting one, we can measure how well a rule that always predicts a training average performs on new observations.

title: Would More Examples Help?
blurb: Before collecting more data or choosing a more flexible model, we can examine how training and validation errors change as the training set grows.

title: When Should a Probability Become an Action?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A probability is evidence, not a complete instruction. We need to decide how likely a sensor failure must be before an inspection is worth its cost.

title: Does Eighty Percent Mean Eighty Percent?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A model can rank failures well and still overstate its probabilities. We need to compare its confidence with what actually happens across similar predictions.

title: Have We Really Held Out a New Example?
blurb: Several rows can belong to the same greenhouse, patient, or device. If we want to predict for a new entity, a random row split can put familiar entities on both sides of the evaluation.

title: What Changed After the Model Was Fitted?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: A model tested on one mix of conditions may later face another. Comparing the incoming data with the reference data helps us notice changes without pretending that every change proves an accuracy failure.

title: How Much Does Our Estimate Depend on This Sample?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: One average hides how it might change if different observations had been collected. Resampling the observed data gives us a way to study that dependence under explicit assumptions.

title: What Does an Alarm Tell Us?
blurb: An alarm may catch most faulty sensors and still be wrong surprisingly often. We need to know how common faults are before deciding what an alarm means.

title: Which Rule Could Have Produced These Observations?
blurb: A probability rule predicts possible observations. Likelihood holds the observations fixed and compares the rules that might have produced them. That distinction connects probability to fitting a model.

title: Naive Bayes
blurb: A warm casing and an unstable reading may each suggest a faulty sensor. We need a way to combine those clues, while being explicit about what we assume about their relationship.

title: Support Vector Machines and Margins
blurb: Several lines may separate the same labelled examples. We need a reason to prefer one, and a way to handle examples that cannot all be separated cleanly.

title: Hierarchical Clustering
blurb: A collection can have small groups inside larger groups. Joining the closest groups one step at a time lets us inspect that hierarchy without choosing one group count at the outset.

title: Density-Based Clustering
blurb: Groups need not form round clouds, and isolated observations need not belong to any group. We can instead ask where enough neighbours support extending a cluster.

title: Images as Arrays
blurb: Before a computer can find a seed in a photograph, it needs measurements to work with. We will look at the rows, columns, channels, and number types that make up an image.

title: Image Thresholding
blurb: A bright seed on a dark tray gives us a first rule to try. Compare each pixel with a cutoff, keep the result as a mask, and inspect where that rule fails.

title: Cleaning Masks With Morphology
blurb: A threshold can leave speckles and gaps. We can test a small shape against the mask to remove or connect particular structures, provided we understand what else that operation will change.

title: Connected Components
blurb: A mask tells us which pixels were selected. To count regions, we need a definition of connected and a way to give each reachable group its own label.

title: Image Augmentation
blurb: The same seed can appear in several positions or orientations. We can teach a model which changes should preserve an answer, but the transformation must keep the image and its labels consistent.

title: Transfer Learning
blurb: A model trained on other photographs may already measure useful visual patterns. We can test those features with a new prediction head before deciding whether the feature extractor also needs to change.

title: Bounding Boxes and Overlap
blurb: Knowing that a seed appears in a photograph does not tell us where it is. Rectangles give us a location to predict, and overlap gives us a way to compare that prediction with a labelled target.

title: Non-Maximum Suppression
blurb: A detector can report several rectangles around the same seed. We will rank candidates, keep a strong one, and remove sufficiently overlapping alternatives while preserving candidates for other objects.

title: What Would We Predict Before Fitting Anything?
blurb: Tomorrow's water demand is unknown. Yesterday's demand gives Botie a prediction he can actually make, and a reference that a more complicated forecast should improve on.

title: Building Inputs From Earlier Days
blurb: A prediction row needs information available before its target. We will turn one ordered record into rows of earlier readings without accidentally including the answer.

title: Separating Repetition From Change
blurb: A demand increase might be a lasting change or a normal part of the weekly schedule. Comparing like positions in a cycle helps us distinguish those possibilities.

title: Updating a Forecast Without Starting Over
blurb: Botie needs to respond to new demand without letting one unusual day replace everything he knows. A weighted update lets him control how quickly his estimate changes.

title: Learning From a Series' Own Past
blurb: A trailing average gives every lag the same influence. An autoregressive model fits different coefficients for the earlier readings and then uses that same rule to predict ahead.

title: Testing a Forecast as Time Moves Forward
blurb: One convenient cutoff can hide a forecasting failure. We will replay several prediction dates, preserving what was known at each one, and compare methods on matching targets.

title: Trying an Action Before Knowing Its Value
blurb: Botie can choose a watering schedule, but sees the result only for the schedule he actually tries. He must balance using his current favourite with learning about alternatives.

title: Describing What an Action Changes
blurb: Watering changes the greenhouse Botie will face tomorrow. A state, an action, and a transition model let us describe that consequence before choosing a policy.

title: Valuing Rewards That Arrive Later
blurb: An action can cost water now and help a plant later. A return combines a sequence of rewards so Botie can compare more than the immediate outcome.

title: Planning One Step, Then the Remaining Journey
blurb: A long sequence of choices is difficult to compare directly. We can combine the reward from one action with the value of the state it leaves behind, then improve those estimates repeatedly.

title: Learning Action Values From Experience
blurb: Botie may not know the transition probabilities. A sampled action, reward, and next state can still correct one entry in an action-value table.

title: Planning for More Than One Possible Outcome
topic: Describing What We Do Not Know
blurb: A delivery might contain different numbers of damaged sensors. Keep the possible outcomes and their probabilities together before deciding how many replacements to hold.

title: Updating an Unknown Failure Rate
topic: Describing What We Do Not Know
blurb: A few failed sensors give evidence about a failure rate, but do not determine it exactly. Keep a distribution over plausible rates and update it as results arrive.

title: Combining Measurements With Different Reliability
blurb: Two thermometers disagree. Their known error variances tell us how strongly each reading should influence a shared estimate.

title: Tracking a State We Cannot Observe Directly
blurb: An alarm does not directly reveal whether equipment is healthy. Combine how states change with how each state could produce the observed alarm.

title: Predicting Between Measurements With Uncertainty
blurb: Botie has measured temperature at only a few positions. A covariance rule connects nearby locations and describes how uncertain an unmeasured location remains.

title: Learning From a Few Records at a Time
blurb: Botie has more training records than he can process in one step. A batch gives him a manageable estimate of the direction in which to change the model.

title: Remembering the Direction of Earlier Updates
blurb: Successive batches can pull a weight in different directions. A stored velocity lets Botie carry some of the previous update direction into the next step.

title: Giving Different Weights Different Step Scales
blurb: Some parameters repeatedly receive larger gradients than others. Adam keeps separate running estimates of gradient direction and squared magnitude for each parameter.

title: Checking a Model Before a Long Training Run
blurb: A network can fail because its starting values suppress the signal or because its derivative is wrong. Test these separately before tuning the optimiser.

title: Deciding When a Training Run Has Done Enough
blurb: Training loss can improve after predictions on unseen records stop improving. Keep separate curves, choose a stopping rule in advance, and restore the best saved model.

title: Recommending Something Before Knowing the Reader
blurb: Botie has a shelf of guides and a record of which were opened. Begin with a popularity baseline, then examine what those records actually tell us.

title: Matching a Reader’s Interests to Guide Descriptions
blurb: Guide descriptions give us evidence even before a guide has been opened. Represent topics explicitly and compare them with a reader’s interests.

title: Learning From Readers With Similar Preferences
blurb: A guide’s description may miss what readers value. Shared ratings let Botie compare preferences, provided missing ratings remain distinct from dislikes.

title: Compressing a Sparse Table of Preferences
blurb: A rating table can be enormous and mostly empty. Small vectors for readers and guides can share information across its observed entries.

title: Checking the List a Reader Actually Sees
blurb: A recommender usually shows a short list. Evaluate that list’s relevant items, their positions, and the cases where little history is available.

title: Finding Unusual Readings Without Letting Them Set the Reference
blurb: A faulty sensor can pull an ordinary mean toward itself. Use a robust centre and spread, then decide what a large deviation actually warrants.

title: Judging a Reading Against Its Neighbours
blurb: Different operating regimes can have different spreads. Local outlier factor compares a point’s density with the density around its neighbours.

title: Finding Readings That Are Easy to Separate
blurb: An isolated reading often needs few random splits to stand apart. Follow paths through small trees before averaging that evidence across a forest.

title: Detecting Patterns a Model Cannot Reconstruct
blurb: A model trained to reproduce normal sensor patterns can expose departures through reconstruction error. The error still needs a validated alert rule.

title: Recording Which Things Are Connected
blurb: A table of pump readings leaves out the pipes between pumps. A graph records those relationships so calculations can use the connections.

title: Following Probability Through a Network
blurb: A random walker chooses among outgoing links. Follow the probability mass to see how graph structure changes where it accumulates.

title: Letting a Node Read Its Neighbours’ Measurements
blurb: A pump’s neighbours can provide useful context. Aggregate their readings while retaining the distinction between a node and its surroundings.

title: Learning From a Node and Its Neighbours Together
blurb: A graph convolution combines node features, self-connections, degree scaling, and learned weights. Work through these pieces before calling the result a layer.

title: Scoring Connections We Have Not Observed
blurb: Node representations can score possible links, but missing links are not guaranteed negatives. Design the split and candidate set before evaluating.

title: Separating a Useful Prediction From a Causal Claim
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: Plants receiving extra water may grow poorly because they were already struggling. Compare the question a prediction answers with the question an intervention asks.

title: Making a Fair Comparison by Assignment
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: Random assignment separates a treatment decision from the reasons a gardener might otherwise choose it. Estimate an average effect while keeping the experiment’s unit and uncertainty clear.

title: Comparing Treatments in the Same Population
blurb: When starting conditions affect treatment choice, standardisation can compare both treatments using one target population, if the measured conditions suffice to control confounding.

title: Reweighting Records Without Inventing Missing Evidence
blurb: Inverse-probability weighting changes which records count most. Understand the treatment probabilities and overlap assumptions before interpreting the resulting contrast.

title: Saving the Whole Prediction Procedure
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: Weights alone do not reproduce a prediction. Botie also needs feature order, fitted preparation, and the rules connecting them.

title: Checking What Arrives at the Model
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: A model can produce a number from the wrong columns or units. Define and validate the request before trusting its arithmetic.

title: Keeping a Prediction Consistent Across Requests
blurb: The same input should have the same preparation and result whether it arrives alone or in a batch. Keep prediction free of accidental fitting and mutable shared state.

title: Knowing Which Model Produced an Answer
blurb: A result needs a link to the model, preparation, data, and code that produced it. Version the prediction procedure so comparisons and rollbacks are meaningful.

title: Checking the Model After It Meets New Data
blurb: Inputs, outcomes, and service behaviour can change after launch. Monitor each separately and keep a tested route back to a known compatible version.

title: Investigate a Sensor Before Calling It Faulty
blurb: Fit a reference from earlier readings, select an alert rule on validation records, and evaluate that fixed rule on later labelled cases.

title: Forecast Tomorrow’s Water Demand Without Seeing Tomorrow
blurb: Build lagged inputs, compare an autoregressive model with persistence, and evaluate both through a sequence of later forecast origins.

title: Count Seeds While Keeping the Image Assumptions Visible
blurb: Turn a small tray image into a binary mask, label connected regions, and investigate when a region count stops matching the number of seeds.
